To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the phosphorus acquisition and use efficiencies of plants from phosphorus-impervished environments are superior to those from phosphorus-rich environments and (ii) this superior efficiency results from a suite of mechanisms that can be divided into two categories, namely those that are related to the root system architecture (RSA) and those related to the physiology of the plant.
“We have identified a new mechanism by which plants adapt to low phosphorus, and we have shown that it is widespread in nature and can be used in agriculture”.

the adaptation of the Australian native shrub, Acacia pycnantha Benth, to low P is associated with a combination of morphological and physiological traits, and that these traits are likely to be the outcome of the evolution of the root system architecture, the root system size and the root system density, as well as the root system plasticity to P availability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms involved in the acquisition and use of P by plants, in order to identify targets for improving phosphorous acquisition and/or use efficiency in crops and model organisms.
the molecular mechanisms involved in plant adaptation to low phosphorus.
understanding how plants adapt and thrive in phosphorus-impervious environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
post-genomic studies are needed for both crops and wild species, to better understand how plants adapt to P-deprivation, and to identify genes that can be used for breeding or engineering.
the study of plants from low-P soils is a promising approach for the development of crops with enhanced P acquisition and/or use efficiency.

the study of plants adapted to low P is a good strategy to understand the responses to P-deficiency and to find targets that could be used to improve P-acquisition efficiency and P-use efficiency of crop species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phosphorus acquisition and use efficiency in plants is a complex trait that involves multiple mechanisms and genes, some of which are conserved and others that are not.
we are interested in the adaptation of plants to low P and how this adaptation is linked to the evolution of plant traits.
we are trying to understand how plants can grow in the absence of phosphorus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adaptation to low phosphorus is a complex trait that is the outcome of multiple genetic changes.
the P-starved bush is a promising source of genes that can be used to improve crop phosphorus use efficiency.
post-genomics is a very useful tool to study the adaptation of a species to low phosphorus availability, in particular when the plant of interest has no genomic resources available.
